opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, because people tend to remember the tensor view stuff, the idea that you have a storage and then strided views on top of it, and that really did come from that lineage. But I think the deeper legacy is a bit more philosophical.

If you go back to SN and then Lush, the system Yann and Léon built in the late eighties and through the nineties, the thing that strikes me is that they treated the framework as a *language environment* rather than a library. You had an interactive interpreter, you could poke at your model, inspect things, and then drop down to compiled code when you needed speed. That combination of interactivity plus performance is basically the thesis of every good ML framework since. Torch carried that forward with Lua, and PyTorch with Python. The eager, "just run it and look at it" style that people credit PyTorch for has very old roots there.

The second piece is the modular abstraction. The idea that a neural network is composed of modules, and each module knows how to do its forward pass and its backward pass, the fprop and bprop, and you just chain them together. That sounds obvious now, but it was a really clean way to think about gradient-based learning as a composition of differentiable blocks. Léon wrote about this quite explicitly, and it shaped how Torch's `nn` package was designed, and in turn how `nn.Module` in PyTorch feels.

And then on Léon's side specifically, the stochastic gradient descent work. He was arguing for SGD at scale long before it was fashionable, when a lot of the community was more interested in convex methods and second-order optimization. The frameworks we build today are essentially machines for running SGD efficiently, so in a sense he defined the workload we're all optimizing for.

So I'd say the legacy is less about any single data structure and more about a stance: research tools should be interactive, compositional, and pragmatic about performance. Those of us who worked on Torch and PyTorch were, honestly, standing on that foundation more than people realize.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, because people tend to flatten both of them into a single headline. Yann becomes "the convnet guy," Léon becomes "the SGD guy," and that undersells what they actually built together, which is the intellectual lineage that PyTorch sits on.

The thing people forget is that in the late eighties and nineties, Yann and Léon were already writing frameworks. There was SN, and then Lush, which was this Lisp-based system they used at Bell Labs. And the design philosophy in those tools is remarkably modern. You had a dynamic, interpreted language at the top, where you'd define your model and iterate quickly, bound to fast compiled numerical kernels underneath. That two-layer idea, a scripting layer over a performance layer, is basically the architecture of every deep learning framework since, Torch7 and PyTorch very much included. They had modules, they had something you'd recognize as a module graph with forward and backward, decades before autograd was a buzzword.

Léon's contribution there is both deep and underrated. He's the one who, with Yann, really nailed the idea that a learning system is a composition of differentiable modules and that you should be able to plug them together like building blocks. The 1998 "Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition" paper has this whole section on what they called graph transformer networks, which is essentially a framework for training structured systems end to end. That's the conceptual ancestor of what we now casually call "just backprop through the whole pipeline."

And then Léon's work on large-scale stochastic optimization gave frameworks their reason to exist in the first place. The argument that you should be willing to trade away precision per step for throughput, that SGD scales where second-order methods don't, is why the entire engineering effort went into fast minibatch gradient computation rather than into, say, better Hessian solvers. Frameworks are built around that assumption. He basically chose what the hot loop would be.

Yann's legacy beyond the architecture itself is cultural, in a way that directly shaped how I think about tools. He pushed, relentlessly and sometimes unpopularly, for the position that the model and the software are not separable, that you can't do good research with bad tools. When he came to Facebook he was very supportive of us working on Torch, and later PyTorch, as a serious research investment rather than as a side project. He also had this strong instinct toward openness. The Lush stuff was open, Torch was open, and that set the expectation that the infrastructure of the field should be shared. I don't think PyTorch being open from day one was a coincidence given who was in the room.

So if I had to compress it: Léon gave us the mathematical justification for how these systems should be built and the modular abstractions to build them, and Yann supplied both the architectures that made those tools worth having and the conviction that building the tools was itself real science. The tensor-level stuff, the views and strides and so on, is downstream of all that. It's the plumbing. The ideas about what the plumbing is for came from them.

astra-6.text:
I think their legacy is much broader than any one feature like tensor views. They helped establish a way of thinking about machine learning software: you want reusable components, you want to compose them, and you want the framework to make experimentation easier without hiding the computation from you.

Automatic differentiation is a good example. The important contribution isn’t just computing a derivative; it’s organizing software so that researchers can build a new model without rebuilding all the machinery around it. That relationship between modularity and experimentation is fundamental to how we think about frameworks today.

I’d be careful about assigning every individual idea to Yann or Léon. But I think their technical legacy is that combination of mathematical clarity and practical systems thinking—making research ideas concrete enough that other people can use them and build on them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think their legacy is much broader than any one feature like tensor views. Yann and Léon were thinking very early about how you build software that makes machine learning research productive: how you represent computation, how you compose modules, and how you get gradients through those modules without rebuilding everything for each experiment.

And that requires a particular balance. You want useful abstractions, but you also want a researcher to be able to look underneath them, change something, and try an idea that the framework designer didn’t anticipate. To me, that’s a really important part of their influence—the framework as a tool for experimentation, where the abstractions serve the research.

I wouldn’t attribute every modern framework idea directly to them. A lot of people contributed along the way. But their work helped establish that way of thinking about machine learning software, and I think that’s a much more substantial legacy than a particular tensor operation.
